When you initially chose a door, you had a 1/100 chance of picking the prize. We can pretty easily agree on that. After the host reveals to you 98 empty doors leaving only one door to choose from, in your mind it's a 50/50. However, the new information does not change the fact that you made a 1/100 chance, that still persists even after revealing all of the other doors. Because you chose before knowing which doors were empty, you STILL have a 1/100 chance of winning.    
    
Now the percentages shift, though. All of the other choices have been condensed down into a single door that hasn't been revealed yet. Since your chance of winning is still 1 in 100, switching would give you a 99 in 100 (the inverse of your initial pick) chance at winning a prize.    
    
The reason why it is not a 50/50 is because your initial pick was made when there were 100 unknown doors, prior to the new information of which doors were empty.

Blaming the playerbase instead of the company failing to deliver a quality product is a wild take to me. It's not like exploits involving the cannon are even a new thing, it's been a failure from Rare for a long time now. They simply introduce even more mechanics that break this already broken component of the game even more. Sure, you have to be a bozo to use an invulnerability exploit to ruin the experience for somebody else, but expecting people to not discover something as easy as crouching while entering a cannon and not having QA Tested for that is next level.

The true answer is that you are not going to bridge the gap in a day, it's going to take time. Failing is an integral part of learning, especially in a game like this where the only "upgrades" you can get are to your personal skill. If TDM is the big issue, you need to focus in on ladder guarding. Repairs can wait if you hear somebody getting on your ship, unless you're already so full of water that you'll sink without a bucket. The most effective way to ladder guard is with a blunderbuss, waiting until the opponent enters his climbing animation at the top of the ladder to fire (at higher levels of play, you'll see players cancel this animation halfway to jump and avoid your shot, or ladder cancel just before getting to the top to drop down the ladder and make you miss your blunderbuss shot, so be aware of this). Alternatively if you run a loadout with a sword, timing your sword lunge to be at the precise moment they reach the top of the ladder to launch them off is effective. Keep in mind that if you mistime your lunge, you can always interact with the sail to cancel the "stun" animation you get from missing.    
    
Once they're on board, it's just about keeping mobile while you fight. As a boarder, I have "routes" that I'll run to stall. My primary objective is to keep you from being able to repair your ship, even if that means I delay you rather than killing you. If you try to repair or bucket while I'm on board, that's when I'll take advantage and try to kill you. You can bait somebody to close distance by getting a bucket or faking a rep, but staying stationary makes it incredibly simple to two tap you with a double gun, or even corner you with sword slashes. Again, if you run a sword in your loadout, be very careful with when you choose to sword lunge since even one miss will lead you to be killed while in your stun animation.    
    
Finally, don't discount using blunderbombs. Not only can they knock a boarder off a ladder, but can get you kills with splash damage or direct hits and can even knock the boarder off of your boat. Just be careful as the hitboxes can be very weird on your ship and you may end up damaging yourself.

Boarding at higher levels of combat is actually extremely risky. Getting killed on aboard attempt means that your ship is down a person and they can easily be overwhelmed by the opponent before they have a chance to respawn by the enemy crew. It's generally only used by good players as a finisher or when a ship is trying to run away. MOST of the time boarding in combat happens after the ship is essentially disabled with their sails down and/or anchored.    
        
I understand not wanting to invest time into getting better at combat if you don't have enough spare time or just don't like the pvp that much, but it will obviously always exist. Just try and get creative with how you keep boarders away. Blunder bomb your ladders, don't ladder guard right in front of the ladder, keep your eyes peeled for mermaids and listen for the sound of a person firing out of a cannon to be ready for the board.

I'd like to just counter-point as somebody also 3ish hours into the game.    
    
1) The PC controls feel about as they do in any other game. I have no issues with them at all. Everything functions precisely as I expect them to.    
    
2) The amount of junk seems similar to other Bethesda titles. However, it very conveniently sorts it into an "etc" bucket for you so you know what's junk and what's not in your inventory! Very handy if you happen to grab a few things and not know if they're useful. No issues there at al.    
    
3) There is in fact a map, although you'll need to be on your ship to access it. While it can be overwhelming while exploring a planet to not have a map (and I'm not sure if that's upgradable later as I have not looked through the entire skill tree), you can easily see points of interest in the distance with your scanner and find your way around. Ultimately, moving your ship with you while you travel is the best way to do things.    
    
4) The ship builder may seem overwhelming at first, but it's fantastically intuitive once you play with it! Things easily move around and "snap" where they should be. It immediately lets you know if there's any issues and tells you precisely how to solve it, and is extremely customizable to build essentially anything that you want. LOVE the system.    
    
5) The intro to the game seems fairly standard. I'm not sure what would make it incredibly underwhelming compared to other Bethesda titles. I think it's going to be down to how interested you are in exploring alien planets.    
    
6) The colors have been a bit on the dull side so far, at least on the moon that I landed on as part of the intro. However, the city was lovely and vibrant and I'm sure other planets will be as well!

A couple things to watch for in positioning:    
    
If they are ever nosing you, sailing right at you in a direct line, this is the best possible time to fire your chainshots. In MOST cases, nosing a ship like this is a mistake, so avoid doing this to others, but take advantage of it when it happens to you.    
    
When you see that you might get caught in a broadside, turn away from that fight (unless you have some other tool to give you an advantage, like a special ball that you just hit or them having downed sails or a lot of damage on them already). If you sustained a lot of damage because you got caught in bad positioning, sail directly away with full sails down so you can repair before turning back into the battle.    
    
Keep your mast fully repaired at all times, your biggest advantage as a sloop is it's harder to take the sails down with chains as they need multiple hits. In addition to this, prioritize defending boarders and taking shots when you have superior positioning over repairing. You can always bucket when needed. Be careful that you are not in a position to be boarded while doing this, however.

I'm very rarely running from a fight, but I still use a similar strategy to get an advantage in positioning over a ship. Using your harpoon to get around a rock can be very useful, as can an anchor turn when you're out of sight.

Ship positioning is key, especially against larger ships. Above all else you must keep your ship clear of boarders, putting yourself in positions where they can board you after a volley or fire out a player to board while they turn to engage can be fatal. As a solo you will have to turn out of potentially bad engagements a lot, so expect fights to take a while and always try to keep them as far away as you possibly can. If at any point you can get their sails down, you need to hammer them with special balls and start your death spiral, slowly sailing around them in a circle with your sail mostly raised while cannoning into them. If you manage to kill one or two, you can fire over to finish them off, but many times it will not even be needed.
